disputed: No court or agency has ruled that any specific donation was an illegal quid pro quo. The documented facts are the correlation between donations and contract awards, the secrecy structure, and the unresolved constitutional question — not a proven bribery conviction.

items: The White House released a list of 37 named donors but acknowledged letting others remain anonymous, and has not disclosed how much each donor gave. (Campaign Legal Center (https://campaignlegal.org/update/challenging-corruption-foundation-president-trumps-east-wing-ballroom))

The contract governing the donations shields donors' identities, excludes the White House from conflict-of-interest protections, and was disclosed only after a watchdog group sued and a judge ordered it released. (Washington Post (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/04/21/trump-ballroom-donor-deal/))

A government watchdog report found that more than half of the publicly identified donors won new or expanded federal contracts worth more than $50 billion in the six months after donating. (Washington Post (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/06/04/donors-won-50b-contracts-after-giving-trump-ballroom-project-report-says/))

CREW's legal analysis found at least 23 donors should have reported the gifts under lobbying disclosure law; only one company (Vantive Healthcare) actually did. (CREW (https://www.citizensforethics.org/reports-investigations/crew-investigations/white-house-ballroom-donations-should-be-disclosed-on-lobbying-disclosure-reports/))

A federal judge has been weighing whether private financing lets the administration bypass the constitutional requirement that Congress approve spending on projects like this; litigation is active, including National Trust for Historic Preservation v. National Park Service. (Washington Post (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/02/09/trump-ballroom-judge-ruling/))

Sens. Warren and Blumenthal introduced the "No Auctioning Off the White House Act" to bar future presidents from funding construction this way, citing that "key ballroom donors currently have business interests in front of the Trump administration." (Sen. Warren (https://www.warren.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/warren-garcia-introduce-new-bill-to-stop-apparent-bribery-involving-trump-ballroom-donations/))
sections.label: Documentation

summary: In October 2025, the East Wing of the White House was demolished to build a roughly 90,000 sq ft ballroom. Cost estimates grew from an initial $200 million to $300-400 million, with Trump and his allies saying they raised nearly $400 million from private donors, including Meta, Coinbase, Ripple and Lockheed Martin.
title: White House East Wing demolition and ballroom private financing
